A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LORE research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across additions, relocations, and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original CLIP and DINOv2 fine-tuning experiments, classification results, corruption evaluations, ablations, and computational measurements in Section 6 and the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds adaptive-margin ablations, supervised fine-tuning results, and ADE20k segmentation evaluation.

M1.justification: The original unsupervised objective, dual network, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Section 6.4 and Appendix J.7 add supervised adaptations combining TeCoA with embedding proximity constraints or an output-distribution KL constraint scaled by reference-model entropy. These extend the existing framework without replacing its central procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix J.8 adds ADE20k semantic segmentation, substantially extending evaluation beyond image classification and embedding alignment. Appendix J.7 also introduces supervised image-label fine-tuning on ImageNet-100. The earlier classification datasets and corruption scenarios remain covered.

E2.justification: TeCoA, previously discussed but not experimentally compared, becomes an evaluated baseline for the supervised variants in Tables 5 and 14. Tables 4 and 13 also introduce fixed-margin LORE comparators. Existing FARE and pretrained-model comparisons are retained; newly discussed RoCL and DeACL are not evaluated.

E3.justification: Existing classification and attack protocols remain unchanged. New experiments introduce fixed-margin sweeps, supervised fine-tuning comparisons, robustness averages across specified attack budgets, and clean/adversarial segmentation mIoU. The supervised training budget is ambiguous: Section 6.4 states five epochs, whereas Appendix J.7 states fifteen for matching reported results.

E4.justification: Tables 4 and 13 add a focused test of sample-adaptive margins against fixed tolerances of 0.6, 0.8, and 1.5. The supervised experiments compare embedding-space and KL constraints. Existing dual-network, K, corruption, and efficiency analyses remain unchanged; the expanded Figure 6 redisplays evidence already present in Figure 7.

E5.justification: The new checklist explicitly acknowledges the absence of error bars and cites the expense of multiple-seed retraining, adding disclosure about uncertainty reporting. Neither version supplies run counts, seed identities, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The checklist's assertion that benchmark diversity ensures significance is not new statistical evidence.

E6.justification: All twelve original tables retain their numerical contents, but Tables 13–15 add substantial new findings. Adaptive-margin LORE2 achieves 31.72 average robust accuracy versus 26.92 for fixed margin 0.8. New supervised results favor the constrained variants. ADE20k clean/attacked mIoU is 0.43/0.35 for LORE8, 0.42/0.23 for the pretrained model, and 0.23/0.15 for FARE8.

T1.justification: Theorem 6.2 and the assumptions, bounds, and proofs in Appendices A, B, E, and F remain unchanged. Appendix J.7 adds formal supervised optimization formulations, particularly the KL constraint with reference entropy defining its tolerance. This is a limited mathematical extension without new theoretical guarantees.

C1.justification: The introduction changes the claim that LORE 'optimally balances' robustness and nominal performance to achieving a 'superior empirical balance'; Figure 1 makes the corresponding qualification. The principal contributions concerning unsupervised robustness, fidelity, generalization, and embedding interpretability remain.

C2.justification: New discussions interpret fixed margins as overly restrictive or overly permissive, explain entropy-dependent KL tolerance through model confidence, and argue that proximity constraints extend to supervised fine-tuning and segmentation. The existing explanations of training stability and the main limitations are largely retained.

D1.justification: The additions document fixed-margin values, supervised class-text templates, learning rate 1e-5, constraint parameter 0.1, and the segmentation benchmark source. Original Appendix C settings and computational details are unchanged. Reproducibility of the supervised addition is weakened by conflicting five- versus fifteen-epoch descriptions.

R1.justification: Related work adds RoCL and DeACL, foregrounds the existing connection to Robey et al.'s constrained learning, and removes several general attack and VLM references. The segmentation experiment adds Kowalczuk et al.'s benchmark citation. FARE remains the principal unsupervised comparison and the central research positioning is retained.

P1.justification: V2 adds Section 6.4 in question-and-answer form, Appendix J.6–J.8, and a NeurIPS checklist. Related work is rewritten and several claims and explanatory passages are edited, but the original method exposition, main section sequence, and most appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 4, 5, and 13–15. Figure 6 becomes a larger two-panel comparison incorporating the FARE4 plot already shown in Figure 7, with an expanded caption. Other tables are renumbered or relocated, while the original visual designs and most figure layouts are preserved.

improvement.justification: The new margin ablation directly supports a previously untested design choice, while supervised and segmentation experiments broaden applicability evidence. Qualifying the optimality claim as empirical also improves calibration. These benefits provide a limited net improvement, tempered by conflicting epoch counts for matching supervised results and the new checklist's unsupported assertion of statistical significance without uncertainty estimates.
